# Global intrinsic ball lift of normalized thin-fiber laws

Historical claim of scope (pending review here): exact representation theorem. Positive surviving fibers
may have different affine support directions and different dimensions.
Their common-normalized weak law nevertheless has an exact compatible
convex lift with the SAME intrinsic fiber dimension m. The lift uses
one added Euclidean space; it does not choose unrelated coordinate
systems in different fibers. This is a representation of the weak
law, not recovery or continuity of the prelimit maximal depths.

## 1. Hypotheses and conclusion

Fix k>=0 and m>=1. For each l let C_l be a compact convex set in
R^k times R^m, with all its nonempty integer fibers indexed by the
same finite set P subset Z^k. Write K_(z,l)=(C_l)_z, and assume all
these fibers lie in one bounded continuous-coordinate region. Put

    M_l=sum_(z in P)|K_(z,l)|_m>0,       M_l ->0.

After taking a subsequence suppose the fibers have nonempty Hausdorff
limits K_z and the finite measures

    mu_(z,l)=1_(K_(z,l)) dx/M_l -> mu_z

converge weakly. Zero m-volume fibers simply contribute zero measures.
Set p_z=mu_z(R^m), and retain P_+={z:p_z>0}. Then sum p_z=1.

For each z in P_+, there is a compact convex set L_z in
R^m_x times R^m_y with the following properties:

1. Every L_z has intrinsic affine dimension EXACTLY m and intrinsic
   H_m-volume p_z.
2. Projection (x,y)->x sends H_m restricted to L_z exactly to mu_z.
3. For EVERY integer barycentric representation by positive sources,

       j=sum_i lambda_i z_i, lambda_i>0, sum_i lambda_i=1,
       z_i in P_+,

   one has j in P_+ and sum_i lambda_i L_(z_i) subset L_j.
4. The convex hull H of the lifted integer fibers has EXACTLY the
   fibers L_z at its integer bases, and no integer bases outside P_+.

Consequently the original surviving mixed law is the projection of
the intrinsic H_m mixed-volume law of H. Moreover H admits an exact
relative affine-hull reduction to a full convex body in
R^(k') times R^D, where

    k'=dim aff(P_+)<=k,       m<=D<=2m.

The base reduction is a saturated lattice coordinate change. The
continuous restriction at each fiber is an isometry, so H_m is
preserved, with no base-dependent Jacobian. The integer fibers of
the reduced body still have intrinsic dimension m; D need not equal m.

## 2. The weak support is exactly the Hausdorff fiber limit

For z in P_+, the conditional probabilities
nu_(z,l)=1_(K_(z,l))dx/|K_(z,l)| converge weakly to mu_z/p_z.
Their supports converge to K_z. The weak limit has support EXACTLY
K_z, including its boundary and every exposed point.

Here is a useful direct proof, also covering varying thin directions.
Suppose K_l subset B(0,R), R>0, and K_l->K. For x in K choose
x_l in K_l with x_l->x. Given rho>0, choose a fixed
0<t<min(1,rho/(4R)). For large l,

    (1-t)x_l+t K_l subset K_l intersect closed B(x,rho).

The homothetic copy has relative uniform m-volume t^m, independently
of the eccentricity of K_l. Upper Portmanteau on the CLOSED ball
therefore gives nu(closed B(x,rho))>=t^m>0. Repeating with smaller
rho proves x belongs to the weak support. The reverse inclusion
follows from Hausdorff convergence and neighborhoods disjoint from K.

Write E_z=aff K_z=b_z+U_z and q_z=dim U_z. Since |K_(z,l)|<=M_l->0,
Hausdorff volume continuity implies q_z<m. For q_z>0 we obtain
elementarily, under the present bounded actual-body hypotheses,

    mu_z=f_z H_(q_z)|_(E_z),
    f_z^(1/(m-q_z)) is concave.                         (1)

The density has a bounded upper semicontinuous representative on the
compact support K_z, positive and continuous in its relative interior.
Here is a direct construction, using the single-fiber case of Section 5
of `candidate b9e8ea5c75ef1e0e`.
It avoids importing a concave-measure classification theorem.

Fix this z, put q=q_z and r=m-q, and project orthogonally onto E_z.
In the fixed decomposition U_z plus U_z-perp, replace every r-section
of K_(z,l) by a centered r-ball with radius

    [vol_r(section)/(M_l kappa_r)]^(1/r).

Call the resulting q+r dimensional body A_l. Its radius function is
concave by Brunn--Minkowski, and is upper semicontinuous by compactness
of the original sections. Its projection is the projection of K_(z,l),
which converges to the full relative q-dimensional K_z. Thus those
projections contain a fixed q-ball of radius rho>0 for all large l.
They also remain in a fixed bounded region. Fubini gives

    |A_l|=|K_(z,l)|/M_l -> p_z>0,

and its projected volume law is precisely the projected mu_(z,l).
If H_l is its largest hidden radius, concavity makes the radius at
least H_l/2 on a q-ball of radius rho/2, by averaging a maximizer
with the fixed projection ball. Therefore

    1>=|A_l|>=kappa_r(H_l/2)^r kappa_q(rho/2)^q.

The A_l are uniformly bounded. Blaschke selection gives a compact
convex subsequential limit A, with |A|=p_z>0 by volume continuity.
Its indicators converge in L1. Projection of its volume law is mu_z,
because the latter is supported in E_z and the prelimit projected
laws converge to it. Rotational invariance of the hidden sections
passes to A, so these sections are centered r-balls. Their radius
R(x) is bounded, concave, and upper semicontinuous on K_z. Consequently
f_z(x)=kappa_r R(x)^r proves (1) with the stated boundary representative.
Full dimension of A makes R positive in the relative interior of K_z.

This construction is used only to identify each density; it does not
choose independently normalized masses or claim compatibility across
the different decompositions. That compatibility is proved below from
the full common-normalized laws. If q_z=0, the support statement already
gives mu_z=p_z delta_(b_z), without a density theorem.

## 3. Every integer incidence aligns its surviving direction spaces

This section supplies the incidence rule proved quantitatively in
Section 3.1 of
`candidate c0cb4d49afb99df3`.
We include a shorter containment-based proof sufficient here.

First, if j=sum_i lambda_i z_i with z_i in P_+, compatibility and
Brunn--Minkowski give

    p_j >= (sum_i lambda_i p_(z_i)^(1/m))^m>0.            (2)

The intermediate integer base is an actual base in P, since it lies
in the projection of C_l. Thus P_+=conv(P_+) intersect Z^k.

Fix a source z=z_i of positive coefficient lambda=lambda_i. Choosing
one point in each other source fiber gives a translation t_l with

    lambda K_(z,l)+t_l subset K_(j,l).                   (3)

For large l, |K_(z,l)|>=eta M_l for one eta>0, whereas
|K_(j,l)|<=M_l. Thus the target/source volume ratio is at most 1/eta.

We use the elementary fact: if lambda A+t subset B are convex
m-bodies and |B|<=C|A|, then their widths satisfy

    lambda width_A(u)<=width_B(u)<=H width_A(u)           (4)

with H depending only on m,lambda,C. To prove this without a
condition-number assumption, choose a maximum-volume inscribed
simplex of A and map it to the standard simplex. Replacing one
vertex by an arbitrary point of A shows that every coordinate lies
in [-1,1]. The standard simplex contains a ball about its centroid
of radius 1/((m+1)sqrt(m)). Hence a further translation and scaling
put

    B_2^m subset A' subset R B_2^m,    R=m(m+2).

Translate B' so it contains lambda A'. Then
|B'|<=C kappa_m R^m and lambda B_2^m subset B'. For any point v in B',
the cone joining v to the radius-lambda (m-1)-ball through zero
perpendicular to v lies in B'. Its volume is
kappa_(m-1)lambda^(m-1)|v|/m. Consequently B' subset H B_2^m with

    H=m C kappa_m R^m/[kappa_(m-1)lambda^(m-1)].

Since B_2^m subset A', taking difference-body supports proves (4).
For m=1 the perpendicular ball is a point with H_0-volume one, and
the same segment/cone calculation holds.

Apply (4) to (3), then pass to Hausdorff limits. A directional width
of K_z vanishes exactly when the corresponding width of K_j vanishes.
Therefore U_z=U_j. This applies to EVERY positively weighted source:

    U_(z_i)=U_j=:U,      q_(z_i)=q_j=:q.                (5)

The affine offsets align in the required anchored way as well.
Passing the original Minkowski inclusion to the limit gives
sum_i lambda_i K_(z_i) subset K_j. Its affine hull has direction U
and contains the average of any source points. Since every source
has full relative dimension q in its own E_(z_i),

    sum_i lambda_i E_(z_i)=E_j.                         (6)

Equivalently, projecting any choices of b_(z_i),b_j onto U-perp gives
b_j modulo U equal to sum_i lambda_i b_(z_i) modulo U. This is only
an identity for the given anchored combination. No global affine
shear aligning all supports is assumed or inferred.

## 4. The common-normalized cross-measure inequality

For every finite anchored combination, the limiting measures obey

    mu_j(sum_i lambda_i A_i)^(1/m)
                 >=sum_i lambda_i mu_(z_i)(A_i)^(1/m)   (7)

for compact subsets A_i of R^m with positive source masses.
Before the limit this is ordinary m-dimensional Brunn--Minkowski on
the pieces K_(z_i,l) intersect A_i, divided by the SAME M_l. To pass
to the limit, thicken every A_i by an open epsilon neighborhood.
The resulting Minkowski average is inside the closed 2epsilon
neighborhood of sum_i lambda_i A_i. Lower Portmanteau on the source
open sets, upper Portmanteau on the target closed set, and then
epsilon decreasing to zero prove (7). This applies even when the
sets A_i lie in the lower-dimensional limiting affine supports and
have zero volume in the prelimit bodies themselves.

By (5)--(6), fix q>0 and take x_i in relint K_(z_i), with
x=sum_i lambda_i x_i in relint K_j. In (7) take the q-balls in their
parallel affine supports with centers x_i and radii epsilon a_i.
Their Minkowski average is EXACTLY the q-ball in E_j centered at x
of radius epsilon sum_i lambda_i a_i. Density continuity gives

    f_j(x)^(1/m)(sum_i lambda_i a_i)^(q/m)
       >=sum_i lambda_i f_(z_i)(x_i)^(1/m) a_i^(q/m).    (8)

Set r=m-q>0, normalize sum_i lambda_i a_i=1, and put
b_i=f_(z_i)(x_i)^(1/r), S=sum_i lambda_i b_i. The concave-power
Jensen calculation in Section 6 of the companion note gives

    max_(a_i>0, sum lambda_i a_i=1)
           sum_i lambda_i b_i^(r/m) a_i^(q/m)=S^(r/m),

with equality at a_i=b_i/S. Thus

    f_j(sum_i lambda_i x_i)^(1/r)
                 >=sum_i lambda_i f_(z_i)(x_i)^(1/r).    (9)

The use of H_q in parallel affine planes has no extra Jacobian:
each is a translate of the SAME Euclidean direction U. Boundary
points will be included by closing the interiors of the lifts below.

When q=0, all source and target supports are points and (6) says
b_j=sum_i lambda_i b_(z_i). Formula (7) on these singleton sets
becomes exactly p_j^(1/m)>=sum_i lambda_i p_(z_i)^(1/m).
No zero-dimensional density differentiation is used.

## 5. A global hidden space glues all the intrinsic lifts

Use ONE additional R^m_y with its fixed standard coordinate axes.
For 1<=r<=m let V_r be the span of its first r axes. For z in P_+
put r_z=m-q_z. If q_z>0 define

    L_z={(x,y): x in K_z, y in V_(r_z),
                  |y| <= (f_z(x)/kappa_(r_z))^(1/r_z)}.   (10)

If q_z=0 define instead

    L_z={b_z} times (p_z/kappa_m)^(1/m) B_2^m.            (11)

Each L_z is a compact convex body relative to E_z times V_(r_z).
The x and y spaces are orthogonal, so intrinsic product Fubini has
Jacobian one:

    H_m(L_z)=integral_(K_z) f_z dH_(q_z)=p_z,
    (pr_x)_#(H_m restricted to L_z)=mu_z.                (12)

The point-mass formula (11) has the same identities. Positivity in
the relative support interior makes every lift's dimension exactly
q_z+r_z=m.

In any anchored integer combination (5) forces all involved r_z
to be the SAME r. Thus their hidden spaces are literally the same
V_r, despite unrelated fibers possibly having different r elsewhere.
For interior lift points, the triangle inequality and (9) give

    |sum_i lambda_i y_i|
       <=sum_i lambda_i (f_(z_i)(x_i)/kappa_r)^(1/r)
       <=(f_j(sum_i lambda_i x_i)/kappa_r)^(1/r).

Together with (6) this proves the required inclusion. Arbitrary lift
points follow because each full relative convex body is the closure
of its relative interior. The q=0 version is the same ball-radius
inequality using (11). Hence all anchored finite inclusions hold.

Let H=conv union_(z in P_+) ({z} times L_z). This is compact. Every
point of H at integer base j is a convex combination of lift points
whose bases have barycenter j. Combine repeated occurrences of a
base using convexity of its lift, remove zero coefficients, and use
the proved inclusion. It follows that H_j subset L_j; the reverse
inclusion holds by construction. Section 3 showed P_+ lattice-convex,
so no other integer bases occur in the projection conv(P_+).

## 6. Relative affine-hull reduction with exact lattice and H_m tracking

Choose z0 in P_+, set F=span(P_+-z0), and let k'=dim F. Because F
is spanned by integer vectors, F intersect Z^k is a saturated lattice
of rank k'. Choose its integer basis and extend it to a basis of
Z^k; equivalently apply a unimodular coordinate change after
translating z0. The base affine span becomes
R^(k') times {0}, with its integer points exactly
Z^(k') times {0}. Delete the unused base coordinates.

Write G=aff H after this step. Its direction space projects onto
R^(k'). Let W be its vertical kernel, a subspace of R^(2m), and
write D=dim W. Every m-dimensional fiber direction lies in W, so
m<=D<=2m. Choose an affine section b:R^(k')->R^(2m) whose graph
lies in G. Linear algebra then gives

    G={(z,b(z)+w): z in R^(k'), w in W}.

Choose a linear ISOMETRY T:W->R^D. The affine bijection

    (z,X) -> (z,T(X-b(z)))                              (13)

sends H to a full-dimensional compact convex body H' in
R^(k') times R^D. At each fixed z, (13) is a translation followed
by an isometry on W. Its restriction to every fiber's m-dimensional
direction is therefore an isometry, preserving H_m exactly. The
base coordinate is unchanged, so every integer fiber identity and
every weight p_z is preserved. No determinant of the total affine
map is substituted for this fiberwise intrinsic Jacobian.

The inverse of (13), followed by projection to the original x and
the inverse saturated base embedding, is an affine map Pi. Thus

    Pi_#(intrinsic H_m mixed-volume law of H')
              =sum_(z in P_+) delta_z times mu_z.         (14)

The law on the left already has total mass one. Its fibers need not
have full D-dimensional volume when D>m; the assertion concerns
the intrinsic H_m mixed measure, with maximum fiber dimension m.

## 7. Exact depth transfer, and its limitation

If p is a mixed point of H', every original closed halfspace through
or containing Pi(p) pulls back to a closed halfspace containing p
with exactly the same measure, by (14). If its restriction is
constant, it contains the whole law and the depth bound is immediate.
Consequently

    depth_(weak law)(Pi(p)) >= depth_(lift law)(p).       (15)

The projected point belongs to its original limiting fiber K_z,
because that set is exactly the weak support proved in Section 2.
All integer tilts and all closed-boundary masses are retained in
(14)--(15). This is not a common-plane projection of only part of
the law; Pi recovers its entire original continuous coordinate.

It does NOT follow that the prelimit depths converge to either
side of (15). For example the two thin triangles in
`candidate e306d42187c98e53`
have prelimit maximal depth 2/9 and limiting maximal depth 1/4.
Their limiting densities are (t+1)/4 on perpendicular segments at
adjacent bases. Formula (10) gives two intrinsic triangles with
hidden radius (t+1)/8, each of H_2-area 1/2. Their combined lift has
maximal depth 2/9: each fiber has ordinary triangle depth 4/9 and
an isolating integer tilt supplies a matching cap cover. Projection
raises its maximal depth to 1/4. Thus even this exact representation
is not an equality of maximal depths under projection, and supplies
no automatic recovery of a dense fine lattice or prelimit centers.

The rectangle/optimized-radius arithmetic in the companion verifier
`../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_normalized_thin_ball_lifts.py` still applies to each incidence.
The exact intrinsic triangle calibration is checked separately in
`../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_global_intrinsic_thin_lift.py`.
